questions.q: What is a constraint, as this lesson defines it?
options: Something believed true but not yet verified
A fixed condition the design must work within, not up for negotiation
A diagram showing object relationships
A list of stakeholders involved in a project
questions.explain: A constraint is fixed about the problem itself — a deadline, a budget, a legal requirement, an existing system that can't be replaced. Good design has to fit inside it, not negotiate it away.

questions.q: What is an assumption, as distinct from a constraint?
options: A fact confirmed by the legal team
Something the design currently depends on being true, that hasn't actually been confirmed
A synonym for a constraint; the two terms mean the same thing
A stakeholder's personal opinion about the project's priority
questions.explain: An assumption is unverified — it either gets confirmed (becoming a fact the design can rely on) or turns out false. Treating it as already-confirmed without checking is the mistake this lesson warns against.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say undocumented assumptions are so expensive?
options: Because assumptions are always illegal to make in architecture
Because a design built on unstated assumptions looks identical to one built on verified facts until an assumption turns out false, often after the design is already built
Because writing documentation is more expensive than building the solution
Because stakeholders refuse to read documents longer than one page
questions.explain: Every design has to make some assumptions. The expense comes from making them silently, so nobody questioned them while questioning was still cheap — the failure surfaces only after the design is already built or in production.

questions.q: Which kind of assumption does this lesson specifically call out as the most dangerous to make?
options: One that would take weeks to verify no matter what
One made because verifying it is inconvenient right now, not because it's genuinely believed safe
One that's already written down in a design document
One a stakeholder has explicitly confirmed in writing
questions.explain: An assumption made specifically because checking it would slow you down — "I'm sure that's fine" as a way to avoid friction — deserves the most scrutiny, not the least, precisely because convenience is driving the decision rather than actual confidence.

questions.q: Why should a design document list constraints and assumptions separately rather than mixing them together?
options: Because a reviewer needs to challenge them differently: a constraint review checks whether it's still accurate and respected, an assumption review checks whether it's been verified and what happens if it's false
Because Salesforce's documentation templates require separate sections by rule
Because constraints are always more important than assumptions
There's no real reason; it's purely a stylistic preference
questions.explain: Constraints and assumptions need different kinds of scrutiny from a reviewer, so keeping them separate and explicit gives the reviewer something concrete to push on — an assumption baked silently into a diagram is invisible until it fails.
